utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, case number IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before the witness is sworn in, there is something I want to raise with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness would like to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat, Mr. Forgrave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Mr. Nice sends his apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He is tied up on another matter. He expects to be back in Court this afternoon and sends his apologies. Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Forgrave, your correct name, full name, is Martyn Forgrave, M-a-r-t-y-n, spelled with a "Y"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst in January 1986 and you were commissioned as a British army officer in August 1986; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After receiving additional military training --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel let the witness please make a break between the question and answer. Could you please make a pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have already been reminded to -- for us to break a little bit between our answer and question before the interpretation, please. Mr. Forgrave, you continue at this time to be a British army officer?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I am a Major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you posted?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I am back with my regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Which regiment is that?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: The Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, in October 1992 you were deployed to Bosnia-Herzegovina and you were appointed as a liaison officer there, and that you were part of an advance group responsible for establishing a base in Vitez, or in the Vitez area, from which an infantry battalion could launch humanitarian operations?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's all correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And jumping ahead for the moment to the end of your tour, is it correct that your tour of duty then continued from approximately October 1992 to about the 9th of March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that while the role of liaison officer was somewhat undefined when you arrived in Bosnia, the primary goal was to contact as many local personalities as possible in order to develop UNPROFOR's on-the-ground knowledge and insight into the political and military situation?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct. To facilitate our operations on ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, is it correct that your unit was the first of the British Battalion forces or UNPROFOR units to be stationed in the Vitez area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: It was actually the first British force. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that soon after you arrived in the Vitez area, Colonel Bob Stewart, who was your commanding officer, Brigadier Cummings and you, met three Croats at the Hotel Vitez which you came to know was then Colonel Blaskic's HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many Croat soldiers were present and the Croat flag was flying outside the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart and Brigadier Cummings led this meeting, and the purpose of the meeting was to make arrangements for BritBat to use the Vitez school as a base? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Major, as you have explained to me in the first several days that you were in Central Bosnia, you and several other officers in the advance team toured the Vitez area with the local HVO commander, who was Mario Cerkez, and Sefkija Djidic, who was the local Muslim commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that part of the activities that you were engaged in at that time was the removal of checkpoints that each side had set up in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you met and had these dealings with Mario Cerkez, is it correct, sir, that he was wearing a camouflage uniform with the Croat chequerboard insignia, and he was introduced to you and known to you as the local HVO commander in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand that during your time in Bosnia, Mr. Cerkez for a time went to Novi Travnik, where he replaced another Bosnian-Croat officer named Malibasic, and then during your tour returned back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Certainly Mr. Cerkez took over for Malibasic. I can't remember when he returned back from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that it was apparent to you and to the BritBat officers generally that Mario Cerkez commanded the local HVO troops in Vitez, while Blaskic was the overall commander for Central Bosnia who also had his headquarters in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That was my understanding of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please relate to the Court a particular incident or interaction that you had with Mr. Cerkez in connection with -- I don't want to suggest too much, but something to do with some media coverage or taping or filming of something to do with booby traps.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: During the initial -- well, during the first week we were in Bosnia, there was obviously an outbreak of violence in the town of Vitez. Both Mr. Cerkez and Sefkija were responsible for trying to lower the tension within the town. And one instance there was a report of booby traps near the school, which Mr. Cerkez said that he had removed by his engineers. Mr. Sefkija denied that any booby traps had been laid by his forces. The general consensus was a media stunt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any consensus or assessment as who had staged, if you will, what you just described as a media stunt?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I think it's impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you associate the stunt with one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: By virtue of the fact that Mr. Cerkez's engineers had removed the alleged booby traps and Mr. Sefkia had actually said they didn't exist, it would seem to indicate that Mr. Cerkez's forces had either put the booby traps or said the booby traps were in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been pointed out to me that the transcript, at least momentarily, has stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask again, Major, did you associate this -- I am using your word "stunt" -- with one side or the other, that is between the HVO side or the Bosniak side?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Okay. By virtue of the fact that Mr. Cerkez had said he had removed the booby traps from the school, and Mr. Sefkija had not denied that he had any -- he had laid any booby traps, it seemed to indicate that Mr. Cerkez who was responsible for the stunt. But it's impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you develop any impression about that time about Mr. Cerkez, in terms of his being particularly savvy, if I can use that word, in these kind of dealings or in dealings with the media?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Not really. I mean, my impression at that stage was that Mr. Cerkez and Mr. Sefkija were doing their best to actually lower the tension within the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In that regard, is it correct that at a meeting again involving Mr. Cerkez at the HVO headquarters in Vitez, on the 19th of October 1992, that you also met a man named Pero Skopljak, who was described to you as the military police commander in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that Mr. Skopljak was dressed in civilian clothes on that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you by this time also met the mayor of Vitez who is known as Santic, Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that between the two of you, you found that Mr. Skopljak seemed to be more the wheeler-dealer and to have more influence, at least in the matters that you observed, than Mr. Santic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Santic appeared to be the figurehead, whereas Mr. Skopljak was the power behind the throne, so-to-speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Major, that during your time in Bosnia, you observed that the Bosnian army or the ABiH was poorly equipped and somewhat of what might be described by some as a peasant army, whereas the HVO was much better equipped with weapons, including anti-tank weapons and multiple rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether the Muslim soldiers had any complaints to the effect that while they were the ones most poorly equipped, they were typically the ones being sent to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: It was a common complaint throughout the six months, that they believed they were on front-line duty against the Serbs, whereas a lot of the Croat forces were held back for internal security matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in the Vitez area, did you come to know that there was an artillery piece referred to or called "Nora" that was approximately a 202- or 203-millimetre artillery piece which was based or operated out of a quarry near Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right. It was not far from the school where we were based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was an artillery piece operated by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to know, Major, that the PTT building in Vitez was the main communications centre in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's what I believed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, did you come to understand --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- BritBat more generally, that the HVO was able to listen in on telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Cerkez if there was any way of contacting people outside the country, at one stage, whether I could make a telephone call. He said the PTT building was still in operation. This surprised me, because we were having to use radios with a rebroadcast facility in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We may have been talking a bit at cross-purposes there, jumping ahead of each other. In addition to Mr. Cerkez having pointed you to the PTT building, did you and BritBat have any understanding whether the HVO had the capability of monitoring or listening to telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: As a routine security matter throughout our six months, we wouldn't talk openly on the telephones, as we believed that they had been compromised and we would be listened to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, please, to the 3rd of December, 1992. Is it correct that on about that date, a Danish soldier was kidnapped while jogging close to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Stewart ask the BritBat liaison officers, including yourself, to contact Dario Kordic to seek to arrange the soldier's release?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Well, more specifically, he asked Captain Dundas-Whatley to arrange for the soldier's release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any understanding that the reason that on that particular day that Colonel Stewart may have thought of the notion of approaching Mr. Kordic was because there had been a dinner the evening before at the British officers' mess, if you will, attended by Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the dinner in the mess, or in the tent, was an opportunity in which Colonel Stewart and Mr. Kordic could strengthen their relationship. On the basis of that, Colonel Stewart felt that Mr. Kordic might be able to assist in the release of the Danish soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any other recollection of who else from the Bosnian Croat or HVO side, if you will, was at this dinner other than Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the first time, in fact, that you had met Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I believe it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how he was dressed at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember whether he was referred to as Colonel Kordic or Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. You can't remember if he was addressed as Colonel Kordic, but was he dressed in a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he had any particular group of soldiers or entourage, if you will, with him?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I seem to remember he had number of bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, following this dinner, and again this incident with the Danish soldier, did it come to your knowledge that, in fact, the British liaison officer, Dundas-Whatley, was, in fact, able to have dealings with Kordic which resulted in the Danish soldier being released?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe that to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it fair to say that would be a matter of some discussion among the British officers at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was, in fact, reported back that, as a result of the meetings with Mr. Kordic, that the soldier had been released?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, from not only this, but as we get into the course of your testimony, other meetings with Mr. Kordic, that he often wore a rosary around his neck, with a crucifix?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: He would wear a rosary with his uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the 10th of January, 1993, in Novi Travnik. Is it correct that an HVO commander there named Malbasic complained that the Muslims had arrested some of his -- that is Malbasic's -- soldiers and was holding them on the other side of town; that you when to see the Muslim commander, Lendo, who said the arrested men were policemen from Croatia? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Lendo, the officer Lendo, give you any indication that, in fact, the HVO was holding three Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Not at that stage, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that at some point?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, were you able to arrange an exchange of these two sets of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Tensions were rising in Novi Travnik, and eventually both sides agreed to release their respective prisoners. Mr. Lendo refused to release the weapons belonging to the Croatian policemen, which was actually part of the deal for the release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the individuals themselves were released?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it also correct that about this time, you began noticing that the HVO in the Vitez/Busovaca area was being reinforced with troops coming from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, more specifically for Novi Travnik, because that's where the problems were at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you know or recall that the commander in these -- in charge of these reinforcement troops was a Major Ljubic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that there were approximately, in this group, about 100 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And directing your attention -- I'm just going to lead you up to a certain point here. Do you recall that a certain number of these 100 soldiers were dressed differently than the rest of the group?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, there was a number who were dressed in black uniforms with iron crosses, and there were also a number who had badges denoting the fact they were from Croatia. They had "HV" on their badge, with the Croatian chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the soldiers dressed in black with the iron crosses, did they create any particular impression or cause any kind of association in your mind when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I recall an incident which I went to a meeting in Novi Travnik, in the hotel in Novi Travnik, which was the HVO headquarters. I took a small team which I had as a protection element. I went to meet Mr. Malbasic, and there was no electricity, so the place was lit by candlelight. The soldiers, about 100 of them, a lot of them had been drinking. When we entered the foyer of the hotel, there was a chorus of "sieg heil" and Nazi salutes and a lot of gesticulating towards weapons and saying "UNPROFOR," seemingly to say that we would be their target at some stage. I then went upstairs to a meeting with Mr. Malbasic and left my small team behind in the foyer of the hotel. They were not allowed to go upstairs. During the time they were there, one of the soldiers put a pistol in the sergeant major's mouth. He was one of my protective-elements team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this result in any particular protest from either you to Mr. Malbasic or from the BritBat command?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask, if I could, the usher to show you what's been previously marked as Exhibit Z1529. It may be helpful to put that on the ELMO momentarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, looking at what's been marked as Exhibit Z1529, can you tell us, is that the patch or a similar patch to the one you saw on certain of these 100 soldiers in the Novi Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right. It was by no means all of them wearing a patch; probably a minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, among this group, did you come to learn that there was a German mercenary who apparently spoke English as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this mercenary give you any indication of where some or all of these 100 soldiers had come from?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: He stated to soldiers who were with me that some of the contingent had come from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you then identified or assessed the commanding officer, Mr. Ljubic, as a Croat hardliner who came on quite aggressively?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Ljubic, at some point, say to you that if fighting was required to solve the situation, then fighting there would be?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And said something to you that the Croat people in the town would be protected?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour. We have covered most of what was in paragraph 22, except for the last part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a few minutes ago, Major, that Bosnian Croat troops didn't seem to be going to the front lines; that the Muslims, in fact, complained that they were the ones being sent to the front lines. These troops that arrived from the Mostar area, did you have any assessment whether they were sent to or intended to be sent to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: My impression was that they were there to alter the balance of power within Novi Travnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The balance of power vis-à-vis who and who, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Well, Novi Travnik was split down the middle, exclusively Croat on one side and exclusively Muslim on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Major, that you then saw this same Mr. Ljubic approximately two weeks later at the HVO headquarters at Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see on that occasion on the soldiers that were with Mr. Ljubic, a patch or insignia -- well, can you describe that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I remember they had a green leaf on their patch, with some writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the words "Ludvig Pavlovic"?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I seem to remember the second part, Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell the Court, sir, were there occasions or was there an occasion when you saw this same patch on soldiers which were manning the Dubravica checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Can I just clarify that the checkpoint is the one on the Zenica road, the other side of Vitez, outside of Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: It is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to tell me?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I saw them on the checkpoint which if it is Dubravica it's the one going out of Vitez on the outskirts if you would go to Zenica by the back route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the back road to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you saw this patch on some of those Croats or Bosnian Croat or Croat soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to Mr. Kordic, during your six months in Bosnia, is it correct, sir, that you had dealings or meetings with Mr. Kordic on approximately 20 occasions?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Maybe three times a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would appreciate if the Prosecution wouldn't lead this particular subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time and your interactions with Mr. Kordic or in meetings involving Mr. Kordic, let me ask you again, was he ever addressed or approached, if you will, with any particular military title?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: He was known to hold the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you treat Mr. Kordic in your dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: With a certain degree of respect, because he held the rank of colonel, which was equivalent to my battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you also formed or reached the assessment at that point in time, is it fair to say, that in order to get on or have successful dealings with Mr. Kordic, you felt that it was more helpful to treat him well and respectfully as opposed to not?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, at that stage I had no real reason not to treat him with that respect. And it would actually assist in our -- in us achieving our humanitarian mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this person that you had that dealing with, that you identified in Central Bosnia as Mr. Kordic or Colonel Kordic, can you tell us whether he is in the Court today?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point him out, please?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: With the glasses at the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let the record show, Your Honours, that the defendant or, excuse me, the witness Forgrave has identified the defendant Kordic. Let me go now, Major, to late January of 1993. Is it correct that at that time you and two other British Battalion officers came across a roadblock in the Vitez area, this was on the Busovaca-Vitez road, where a senior Dutch officer had been stopped by HVO soldiers and not allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going to lead you here, but did the HVO soldiers at this roadblock give you any information on whose orders they were acting at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: They said we were not allowed to pass on the orders of Colonel Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you just take us through the rest of that, what happened after being stopped at this roadblock. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Well, the first thing to mention, it was strange that we were not allowed freedom of movement. This was the first occasion I had been stopped and physically prevented from moving within a Bosnian Croat area. We then decided that we would force our way through, mainly due to the fact that once we became hostage to every single roadblock, our humanitarian mission would fail. So we drove through with our Land Rover. The two Croat soldiers or Bosnian Croat soldiers raised their weapons and pointed them at us but did not fire. We then carried on to Busovaca to the PTT building where we met Mr. Kordic. Mr. Kordic apologised and stated that the roadblocks were in place to stop Muslim aid agencies smuggling weapons. And he had the roadblock removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see in your presence or make any observations as to any steps that Mr. Kordic took to have the roadblock removed?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: He made a telephone call, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me move forward to about the 28th or 29th of January 1993. You were accompanying Major Jennings at that time at a meeting at the DutchBat headquarters in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you meet or see at this meeting a man called Ante Sliskovic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. He was a regular feature at my meetings with Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, here again, Major, I am not going to lead you through some of this. I just simply want to ask you some questions, and if you can amplify, please. What did you observe about any relationship between Mr. Sliskovic and Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Mr. Sliskovic appeared to be the confidant and sounding board of Mr. Kordic, but Mr. Kordic was clearly in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In some of your own previous discussions and statements on this matter, sir, is it fair to say that you have used the word that Mr. Sliskovic was Dario Kordic's right-hand man?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to the leading nature of that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Don't lead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding or observation of Mr. Sliskovic's role or position, if you will, in the Busovaca-Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: He was responsible for internal security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your own assessment or observation of Mr. Sliskovic and any information about him that was known to the British Battalion at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: My personal impression was he was a deeply unpleasant individual. There were rumours from people I had met and through my interpreters that he had been responsible --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to rumours, Your Honour. Obviously, that kind of unreliable hearsay is not of assistance to any one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me see if I can ask some additional questions, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, if you could limit yourself from what we might call rumour. If you can, can you tell us whether there was discussion, if you will, official discussion among the BritBat officers, the intelligence officers, et cetera, about information gained about various personalities in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: In statements given to myself through my interpreter, in my dealings within the six months I was in Central Bosnia, I was told that he had been responsible for various "atrocities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you simply comment on whether, in your meetings with Mr. Kordic, was it more or less the case that Mr. Sliskovic would also be present?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. My question was, was it more often the case that Mr. Sliskovic was present at these same meetings with Mr. Kordic or only rarely?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Almost entirely he was with Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am directing your attention to the 5th of February 1993. I am at paragraph 30, Your Honour. Is it correct that you went to see Mr. Kordic at his headquarters in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to please show you what's been marked as Exhibit Z1691, 1697 and 1698. I suppose if we could start with -- whichever one is fine. Just see what you have here. All right. For the record, Exhibit Z1691 is on the ELMO. Can you tell the Court, Major, is this the building where you met with Mr. Kordic on the 5th of February 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's where all the meetings were conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the location that you associate -- what they would call at least one of Mr. Kordic's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: This is the -- yes, this is the headquarters I met with Mr. Kordic on every single occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what is shown, is it not, in Exhibit Z1691, is a photograph of what some people would say is the PTT building in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look then again momentarily at Exhibit 1697. Is that also a photograph of the PTT building in Busovaca where Mr. Kordic's headquarters were located?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same regarding Exhibit 1698; is that a third photograph of the same building?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, specifically in connection with the 5th of February, did you meet with Mr. Kordic at any particular location in that building?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I always met Mr. Kordic in his office, which was down two flights of stairs and on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This office was below ground level?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't answer that with any degree of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you walked in at the entrance which was shown on the photographs, and you said you walked in the entrance and you went down two flights of stairs?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: It might have -- sorry. The room didn't have windows, as you could see out of them. It may have had slits at the top, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court what you saw in this particular room in terms of what was on the walls; the trappings of the room, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: There was a map, I think it was a 1-20.000, probably a JNA map, which was marked up with the current military situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a professional military officer, sir, did this room appear to you to have any particular type of room or any particular type of operation associated with it?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Up to that stage, I considered it very much Mr. Kordic's office. At that stage, the current military situation was that the Bosnian forces were surrounding Busovaca and there was a possibility of it becoming a Croat enclave. Mr. Kordic pointed out the current front line, which seemed to suggest that Busovaca was surrounded, and there were a number of arrows depicting the various pressure points on the Busovaca encirclement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say arrows. Just so the record is clear, are you talking about arrows on the map?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Marked in red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to characterise this room at that point in its configuration as an operations room?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I object to the leading nature of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't lead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you can recall about the way that the room was set up at that particular time? Anything else you haven't told us already?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic stated that they were able to intercept ABiH radio traffic, and some of the intercepts seemed to suggest or certainly suggested to him that they had extremist forces to which he referred to as the Mujahedin. There was a fax machine in the corner. To me, he was able to receive information about the current military situation from that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether on that occasion Mr. Kordic showed you any particular items in connection with his discussions with you about the military situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kordic was clearly distressed by the situation and the presence of Mujahedin in the area. And as further evidence he showed -- I suppose it would be an Islamic prayer with a picture on it, which he said had been taken from a Mujahedin soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a fax machine in the room. Can you say anything more about it? Did Mr. Kordic show you any particular fax?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: No. I mean, I think, as I recall, he had a fax in his hand, but I didn't read the text or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without having read it, did he describe it or say anything to you about it?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Only that they were able to intercept radio traffic, and this was evidence that the Mujahedin were supporting the ABiH encirclement of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, please, whether on occasion Mr. Kordic made some inquiry of you about the ethnic origin of one of your interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I used to always use Dobrila, who was a Serb. I remember taking Dobrila to one of the meetings, and Mr. Kordic said along the lines that if he -- he would deal with Croat interpreters and also Serb interpreters, because they had to be neutral anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any further inquiry made about the ethnic origin of Dobrila?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic knew that she was a Serb. Basically, the message was that he would deal with a Croat interpreter and, if he had to, a Serb interpreter, because they had to be neutral in the geographical position they found themselves. And the suggestion was he wouldn't deal with a Muslim interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am directing your attention to the 23rd of February of 1993. Do you recall a situation, sir, where a Dutch military vehicle was stolen or hijacked near Vitez by persons wearing HVO military police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with Colonel Stewart to go to Vitez to try to recover the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you and Colonel Stewart had some dealings with the local HVO police chief, but soon made the assessment that you were unlikely to get much help from this individual?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. Bearing in mind that the Dutch soldiers had reported the two individuals that had hijacked the car were wearing HVO uniforms. There was a vacuum of information when we went to the police station in Vitez about what could have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of inquiries that same day, were you able to determine more information or learn more information about where the vehicle -- where you at least thought the vehicle had been taken?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: The suggestion was, as I recall, that the HVO police chief in Travnik was responsible. He was believed to have Mafia connections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, did you then proceed to any particular senior Croat official to try to recover the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I went to see Mr. Kordic. I would just like to state, you know, he was very helpful in us dealing with problems such as hijacked vehicles. And if there was one individual who could resolve a problem, it would be Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular in regard to this Dutch vehicle, do you remember any particular conversation or position that Mr. Kordic stated to you when you approached him about this?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I think, yes. He stated that he didn't believe it would have been HVO soldiers who would have hijacked the vehicle, but he would do his best, I think, to get the vehicle back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened either that day or the next day?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I think it was the following day, the vehicle was returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that, to your knowledge, Mr. Kordic contacted Major Jennings, who went to -- who then went to Vitez or to where Kordic was located and Mr. Kordic handed over, essentially, the vehicle and its keys?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, certainly Major Jennings collected the vehicle from, I think, Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there a second or at least a further similar incident involving a stolen ITN, which was a news agency, a stolen ITN vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember the exact date it was stolen, but again I arranged a meeting with Mr. Kordic, who was extremely helpful in returning the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In finishing up here, Major, can you just tell the Court in your own words, your own assessment, of the -- who appeared to you during your six months in Central Bosnia to be the principle decision-maker or authority figure in that area?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was the political military figure and he was the man I dealt with for matters of a serious nature because he was and seemed to be able to influence the local situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you may have indicated earlier, is it correct to say that you met with Mr. Kordic directly something around 20 times during your tour?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. I was there for, I think, just under six months, and maybe three times a months, which make it 18, 20 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your observation or knowledge, or BritBat's assessment for that matter, of the relationship between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't recall the actual assessment as such, a formal BritBat assessment of the relationship between Blaskic and Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your assessment?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: My assessment was that Colonel Blaskic was the principal military figure, Mr. Kordic was the political military figure, and as the situation developed and intensified, Mr. Kordic seemed to assume more of a military persona, if you like, and tended not to use Colonel Blaskic, because I found Mr. Kordic an awful lot more effective in dealing with various problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am looking at the transcript, Major. Just to be clear, when you said "tended not to use Colonel Blaskic" you are saying you tended not to use Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, me. But Colonel Stewart, because he was, obviously, spent -- I was visiting lots of personalities on the ground. My commanding officer was based in Vitez, so he was on the doorstep of Colonel Blaskic's headquarters. So he would obviously visit him an awful lot more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your role as liaison officer, you are telling us that the person you would go more directly to would be Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, we have already been over this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought it was a bit confusing, frankly, the way it came out. I am trying to clarify, Your Honour. I think we are completed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your assessment of Mr. Kordic as a leader, as an individual, based on your own dealings with him and what his -- if you will, reputation in the community?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I think he was well respected by the Bosnian Croats and equally, I think, he was feared by the Bosnian Muslims, or his reputation made them fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When people came into rooms with him or were participating in meetings with Mr. Kordic, can you just describe to the Court how the other Bosnian Croats or the Muslims in the room for that matter would act toward or with Mr. Kordic? Just based on what you saw.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I think the Bosnian Croats would give him respect and deference that his rank and position gave him. I can't recall Muslims in the room reacting one way or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your dealings with the Muslims in Central Bosnia, did you have any assessment of, if you will, who they were more concerned about in terms of on the Bosnian Croat side? Mr. Blaskic, Mr. Kordic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to the speculative nature of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness -- we allow hearsay. The witness can say what he was told. Now, what we make of it is a matter for us. Now, let's try and get on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is my final question, Your Honour. If you can help us with that, Major, please do. If not, we'll be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major, just tell us, if you would, what were you told by Muslims about their views of Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: They feared him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major Forgrave, my name is Steven Sayers, together with my colleague Mr. Naumovski we represent Mr. Kordic and the gentlemen to my left are Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Mikulicic, and they represent Mr. Cerkez. Since we both speak the same language, Major, it would be very helpful if you could just pause briefly between the end of my question and your answer, and I will try to do the same, bearing in mind the interpreters. Sir, you yourself do not speak Croatian, do you?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that some of your interpreters were of fairly poor quality, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Some of the interpreters were of poor quality, but those were usually confined to administrative posts, whereas the interpreter I used was also used by Colonel Stewart, Dobrila, and she was of high quality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you gave a statement to the investigators who worked for the office of the Prosecution on April the 26th and April the 28th, 1995, approximately four and a half years ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You actually had some notes available to you to refresh your recollection, I believe, sir, and they were faxed to you on the 27th of April of 1995 from Tessa Kennedy Design, apparently in England, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any other notes apart from these contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: No, those were the notes I made for the first week, and I found myself too busy to continue with the note-taking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, sir, that your first meeting with Mr. Kordic, I think you've testified to this, was at the dinner on December [Realtime transcript read in error "November"] the 2nd of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I believe that to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for the first two months of your tour in Central Bosnia, you had had no meetings with him at all?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you were 27 years old at the time of your tour in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, I believe, were one of four liaison officers in the Vitez region -- actually, one of three; Captain Hughes, I believe, was deployed to Gornji Vakuf. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I think there were five in total, but it covered from Tuzla right down to Gornji Vakuf. My specific area covered Novi Travnik, Travnik, Vitez, up to Zenica -- but not including the town -- and then down as far as Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, one minor item on page 36, line 23. I think the date "November the 2nd" should actually read "December the 2nd." That was the date that the major first met Mr. Kordic at a dinner, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that your area of responsibility basically overlapped with Captain Dundas-Whatley's; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Overlapped in the sense that I had to return to England early to pursue my career course in examinations for promotion. He took over my area. But until that time, they didn't overlap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you were away on leave, I believe, from December the 19th to December the 29th of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yeah. He stood in for me whilst I was away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your duty was, as you've said, to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid to needy persons in your area of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, that was our mandate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That mandate was geared directly to aiding U.N. sponsored organisations in the delivery of that aid, was it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, but it didn't exclude assisting other humanitarian agencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But BritBat was not authorised to provide armed escorts to purely private convoys, though, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Not specifically, but I think it was a matter of interpretation for the commanding officer at that stage. He believed that his mandate sanctioned him to escort non-U.N. convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a written mandate, or was this just the understanding of the commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: He was obviously working from the U.N. mandate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in writing, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: He would have received it in writing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see it?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't recall seeing it. I may well have done. The commanding officer would obviously use the mandate and then -- to design his plan and give his orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few questions in connection with your role as a liaison officer, Major. Would it be fair to describe the process of information collection as a learning process and as evolutionary?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Could you just explain "evolutionary"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You learned more about the local political situation and the military situation as time went on; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, you passed on your knowledge of the information that you had gathered about the political and military situation in your area of responsibility to Captain Dundas-Whatley when you left on March the 9th, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had actually taken over from you in late February of 1993, had he not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that you found Captain Dundas-Whatley to be a capable and knowledgeable liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a perceptive observer, such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you both worked closely together and talked about what you had found out about the situation and passed that information between yourselves, as with the other liaison officers; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't work in isolation. We were debriefed every time we went out, and we were also given access to the information they had gained during our visits, so we had a more complete picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of the information-gathering aspects of your duties, Major, would it be fair to say that you turned over all information that you found to be of significance to the military information cell each evening?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That cell was headed up, I believe, by Captain Chris Leighton, ably assisted by Sergeant James Connelly?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, in this regard, every meeting of significance, every event of significance, would be reported by you to the military information cell, which in turn would prepare contemporaneous summaries of the information related to the cell by you and your fellow liaison officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: My duty was merely to state my impressions and state about various events that had happened that day. I can't vouch for whether the intelligence cell recorded word for word every single visit that I conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Major, but basically the -- correct me if I'm wrong: The military information cell prepared each day, or each evening, military information summaries or milinfosums, and they basically provide, at a snapshot in time, the evolutionary state of the knowledge that you and the other liaison officers had gathered in the course of their work, along with other events of significance; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: It was a summary, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These milinfosums would be updated on a fairly continuous basis, would they not?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Occasionally the information discovered was found to be incorrect and subsequently corrected; correct? Is that accurate to say?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I suspect that might be the case. I don't know. I was never responsible for correcting them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Your principal area of focus in your area of responsibility was from Turbe to Travnik, north up to Guca Gora, and then down to Novi Travnik and east to Vitez, with an occasional visit to Busovaca; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: We took over responsibility for Busovaca at the request of the Dutch transport battalion, so merely my area was extended. So once it was extended, I tended to visit Busovaca when I needed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the request from DutchBat came to your commanding officer in January of 1993; correct? When the tensions started rising in the Busovaca area and actually a conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I thought it was slightly earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that this was an extremely large area for a single liaison officer, and that's why Major Jennings essentially filled in for you during a three-week period in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, I can't remember when Major Jennings filled in for me, but yes, it was a large area, and I tended to go where I was needed or where the problems were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as your duties were concerned, Major, the principal problems were really up on the front lines in the area of Travnik and Turbe; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That was just part of the problem. There were also problems in Novi Travnik, just as there were problems east of Busovaca. There were a number of problems I dealt with, and there were a number of problems in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. One very brief question on artillery resources, sir: There is no question that both sides actually had artillery resources, is there? In fact, I believe you may yourself have reported that the Armija forces, the ABiH forces, had a 152-millimetre artillery piece in their arsenal?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I may well have -- yeah. I can't recall that, but you're -- you're probably right. The only point I would make is that certainly when we first started, that the HVO were better equipped and better trained as a military force, in my military judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher would show you a document that has previously been marked as Exhibit D45/1. And while that's being located, Major, I'll just let you know that that is a copy of milinfosum number 70, dated January the 9th of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three very brief questions on this document. Under the first item on page 1, under the "Travnik" entry, right at the end, it is recorded that the LO reported that a BiH heavy artillery piece, 152-millimetre or larger, was believed to be located to the east of the hospital in the north of the town. Were there any other liaison officers at this area apart from yourself, or does this refer to a report that you, in fact, made?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember submitting this report. I could well have submitted it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware, sir, that combatants had actually been spotted wearing a variety of uniforms, anything that was really available, including British uniforms? Perhaps that's not a clear question, Major. Why don't you turn to the second page under item 5, the Vares entry. Were you aware that some of the units within the Cheshire Regiment had actually seen soldiers in the Vares area who had been dressed in surplus British uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: No. I had heard statements that a variety of uniforms were used. I can't really recall, in my area, ever seeing any British uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you would just turn to the last page, sir, under the last entry, right at the bottom of that page, let me just ask you, the people that you saw in the Novi Travnik area, the minority of the 100-or-so soldiers about which you have given testimony and who were dressed in black uniforms, that was not the first time that people had been spotted wearing black uniforms on either side, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: There had been reports that HOS had been seen in black uniforms. Again, I can't remember any ABiH soldiers being seen in black uniforms. It could well have been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at the milinfosum, I'll read it to you: The recce call sign passed 8th Brigade headquarters and stopped at the main headquarters at Hotel Borac, and then there is a grid reference. At the HQ, there were approximately 40 to 50 soldiers in black uniforms. They were called the Black Swans, and referred to themselves as special forces. These were ABiH forces; correct, Major?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know where that grid reference is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that jog your memory about discussions between you and your fellow liaison officers about ABiH special forces having been spotted wearing black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I had certainly heard of the Black Swans. I can't recall ever having any discussions whether -- what uniforms they had; neither do I ever recall ever seeing them in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a few questions, Major, about the balance of forces and the location of headquarters. It is true, isn't it, that the HVO forces in Travnik were vastly outnumbered by ABiH forces, in the order of 10 or 11 to 1? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact figures. My impression was, as I stated before, that a lot of them were away on the Turbe front and down west of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher would show you the document that's been marked as Exhibit D101/1, which is a copy of milinfosum number 79, dated January the 18th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can deal with this very briefly, Major. There's a reference to an LO team visiting a BiH exchange officer in Travnik. Was this Major Beba Salko; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: It would have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Major Salko claimed to you that the BiH were much stronger than the HVO in Travnik, and that they had 11.000 soldiers at their disposal in comparison to only about 1.000 HVO soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw nothing to persuade you that that was incorrect, did you?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: As a general observation, I didn't take much stock in, when people gave me figures, whether they were accurate or not. Most figures, in my experience, tended to be inflated for one purpose or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're saying, I take it, is that it was not uncommon for exaggeration and hyperbole to be used by both of the combatant sides which you were having dealings with; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with the third side, too, the Serbs, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Obviously we had less contact with the Serbs, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few questions in connection with the 333rd Mountain Brigade, sir. Were you aware that the headquarters of this brigade had been located in the village of Kacuni, approximately four or five kilometres south of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Sorry, four or five kilometres south, did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: My memory is -- exact details of which brigade were there, et cetera, I can't recall; but yes, I had some dealings, with Major Jennings in that area, with the ABiH commander. I'm sure if you gave me his name, I would recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Dzevad Mekic --

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Mekic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- ring a bell? Mr. Mekic was the commander of the 333rd Mountain Brigade at its headquarters in Kacuni; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that the 333rd Mountain Brigade had located to Kacuni, according to the military information summaries available to the British forces, by January the 15th of 1993, just a week before the fighting erupted in that area?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't recall, but yes. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask the usher to show you Exhibit D102/1. Maybe that will refresh your memory. Major, under item one on this milinfosum dated number 75 January 15, 1993, it's recorded that the BiH Brigade located in Kacuni is designated as the 333rd -- it says Brdska Brigade, but that means Mountain Brigade. That's consistent with your recollection; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also recorded there that the HVO Brigade was called the Brigade Nikola Zrinjska, and commanded by one Niko Jozinovic. Did you ever meet Mr. Jozinovic, the commander of that brigade in Busovaca, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I was present at a number of ceasefire agreements. Whether he was there, I can't recall. I suspect -- I remember Mr. Mekic being present, and I presume his opposite number was there, or certainly his deputy. But I can't remember the exact name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There has been some confusion regarding the date that the 325th Mountain Brigade was formed, sir. I wonder if the usher would just show you milinfosum 80, which I have here, dated January the 19th, 1992. I would like to have this marked as the next Defence Exhibit for Mr. Kordic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D127/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, when you have dealt with this document, we'll take the usual adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have basically two questions in connection with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would turn to the second page, sir, under item number two, "Vitez." The military information cell had actually acquired a document with the stamp of the 325th Mountain Brigade on it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: The milinfosum recites the stamp on the document that's attached to this, and you can see it right on the end of the document, if you wish, was that of the 325th Broska Brigade. I am just trying to locate it. The quality of reproduction is poor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately one inch down in the text. Just after the date, 15 January --

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: The stamp on the document was that of the brigade. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there isn't any doubt that the 325th Mountain Brigade existed as of the date of this milinfosum, which was January the 19th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be a fair assumption. And the headquarters of that formation was in the village of Preocica. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: If that's -- I can remember, I think, going to the headquarters. I can't again remember the exact name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Along the main Busovaca road, out from Busovaca, if you turn right and you go up the hill, I think that was where the headquarters was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time to break, Mr. President. If the Court so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now 'til half past 11.00. One housekeeping matter, and that is tomorrow the Court wishes to start at 9.00 in order to finish rather earlier than usual, shortly after midday, unless that is inconvenient to anybody. And similarly, next week, the 26th of November, we'll have the same hours, beginning at 9.00, finishing at midday. Very well. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Major, we were talking about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were talking about the 325th Mountain Brigade dispositions just before the break. I wonder if the usher would show you another milinfosum identified as Exhibit D61/1. And that's from February the 2nd of 1993. I have a few questions connected with note 1 on the first page, and note 4 on the second page, Major. First, do you or do you not actually recall having direct dealings with the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, Niko Jozinovic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that the area to the west of Busovaca, as of the 2nd of February 1993, was controlled by ABiH forces, namely, those of the 325th Mountain Brigade, as reflected in this milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: The area west of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just to help you out, I would also suggest to you that the area to the east of Busovaca was controlled by the forces of the 333rd Mountain Brigade and by another detachment that we'll come to in just a second, the 7th Muslim brigade. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what the disposition of troops was in February that year, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you just turn to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major, if you can't remember, it's six years ago, it would be perfectly understandable if you say so. Mr. Sayers, we have these documents. If the Major is simply not able to remember, it would be much quicker for you to produce the documents in due course and refer to them through your own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We will try to do so. Let me see if I can jog the Major's memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second page of this document there is a reference there to sources stating that elements of the 7th Muslim Brigade were deployed north of Kacuni, and that at least 80 soldiers from that brigade had been moved to the area about five days earlier. Is that consistent with your recollection, or do you not have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: It is fairly consistent with my recollection. I believe the time scale of when I visited Mr. Kordic's headquarters and his references to the Mujahedin would relate to the 7th Muslimski Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The 7th Muslim Brigade were forces under the command of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, headquartered in Zenica, or at least he was headquartered in Zenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes, he and his headquarters from Zenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself had some dealings with Mujahedins; isn't that correct, sir? You were actually tasked by your commanding officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart, to investigate the execution-style murders of two British mercenaries, Derek Arnold and Ted Skinner, on the 3rd of February, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they had been executed by Mujahedins, had they not?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That was our assessment, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn very briefly, Major, to the chain of command which you talked about. There is no question that the commanding officer of the Central Bosnia operative zone throughout your tour of duty was Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: That was my belief, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is no question equally that he had full military command and control over the soldiers under his command, including the military police and special purpose units, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I think you are overemphasising the point saying "full military control." I would say on both sides, the ABiH and the HVO, did not have full military control over their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is it not true that Colonel Blaskic reported in the chain of command to the chief of the general staff of the HVO in Mostar, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, Colonel Blaskic carried out orders that he was given by the general staff of the HVO in Mostar, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTYN FORGRAVE
utterances.text: I would just like to emphasise that I don't think it was so clean-cut, the chain of command, in the same style as, say, the Dutch call a western army. I can only assume that he carried out those orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher would simply show you Exhibit D91/1. You were asked, Major, to give several opinions as a professional military officer, which clearly you are. I would just like to show you this order issued by the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone on the 16th of January 1993 to various divisions.
